title: A Global Study Reveals a Stronger Temperature‐Cell Size Relationship in Diatoms on Islands Than on Continents
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

To study (i) the differences in mean diatom community biovolume (MDCB) and proportion of large taxa (PLT) between insular and continental communities, (ii) their response to environmental and geographic factors and (iii) their latitudinal patterns.

Location

Africa, America, Europe and the Pacific.

Time Period

Present.

Major Taxa Studied

Stream diatoms.

Methods

We compared MDCB and PLT between islands and continents globally and in two of four study regions (America and Europe). Using random forest models, we assessed and compared the response of MDCB and PLT to environmental and geographic variables, the temperature-MDCB and temperature-PLT relationships and their latitudinal patterns in both islands and continents.

Main Results

The MDCB was significantly smaller on islands than on continents, although the difference was comparatively small. Mean temperature and temperature seasonality were the strongest determinants of MDCB and PLT in communities on islands and on continents at a global scale, whereas at a regional scale, their main drivers varied across regions and systems. Islands exhibited a stronger poleward increase of diatom biovolume compared to continents.

Main Conclusions

Mean diatom community biovolume decreased with mean temperature on both islands and continents globally, but temperature had a more prominent effect on islands than on continents. This supports the temperature-size relationship for diatoms at a macroecological scale, especially on islands. Our results suggest that global warming may reduce the mean biovolume of diatom communities through the replacement of large species by small ones and that this reduction may occur at a faster rate on islands than on continents, with potentially profound effects on ecosystem functions.
